{{Technical|date=February 2021}}
In [[econometrics]], the '''truncated normal hurdle model''' is a variant of the [[Tobit model]] and was first proposed by Cragg in 1971.<ref name="Cragg1971">{{cite journal |last1=Cragg |first1=John G. |title=Some Statistical Models for Limited Dependent Variables with Application to the Demand for Durable Goods |journal=Econometrica |date=September 1971 |volume=39 |issue=5 |pages=829–844 |doi=10.2307/1909582 |jstor=1909582 }}</ref>

In a standard Tobit model, represented as <math>y=(x\beta+u)  1[x\beta+u>0]</math>, where <math>u|x\sim N(0,\sigma^2)</math>This model construction implicitly imposes two first order assumptions:<ref>Wooldridge, J. (2002): Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data, MIT Press, Cambridge, Mass, pp 690.</ref>

# Since:  <math>\partial P[y>0]/\partial x_j=\varphi (x\beta/\sigma) \beta_j/\sigma</math> and <math>\partial \operatorname E[y\mid x,y >0]/\partial x_j=\beta_j\{1-\theta(x\beta/\sigma\}</math>, the partial effect of <math>x_j</math> on the probability <math>P[y>0]</math> and the [[conditional expectation]]: <math>\operatorname E [y\mid x,y >0]</math> has the same sign:<ref>Here, the notation follows Wooldridge (2002). Function <math>\theta (x)=\lambda' </math> where <math>\lambda (x) = \varphi (\chi)/\Phi (\chi),</math> can be proved to be between 0 and 1.</ref>
# The relative effects of <math>x_h</math> and <math>x_j</math> on <math>P[y>0]</math> and <math>\operatorname E [y\mid x,y>0]</math> are identical, i.e.:
: <math>\frac{\partial P[y>0]/\partial x_h}{\partial P[y>0]/ \partial x_j}=\frac{\partial \operatorname E[y\mid x,y>0]/ \partial x_h}{ \partial \operatorname E[y\mid x,y>0]/ \partial x_j} = \frac{\beta_h}{\beta_j}|</math>

However, these two implicit assumptions are too strong and inconsistent with many contexts in [[economics]]. For instance, when we need to decide whether to [[Investment|invest]] and build a factory, the construction [[cost]] might be more influential than the product [[price]]; but once we have already built the factory, the product price is definitely more influential to the [[revenue]]. Hence, the implicit assumption (2) doesn't match this context.<ref>For more application example of corner solution model, refer to: Daniel J. Phaneuf, (1999): “A Dual Approach to Modeling Corner Solutions in Recreation Demand”,Journal of Environmental Economics and Management, Volume 37, Issue 1, Pages 85-105, ISSN 0095-0696.</ref> The essence of this issue is that the standard Tobit implicitly models a very strong link between the participation decision <math>( y=0</math> or <math>y>0)</math> and the amount decision (the magnitude of <math>y</math> when <math>y>0</math>). If a [[corner solution]] model is represented in a general form: <math>y=s \centerdot w,</math>  , where <math>s</math>  is the participate decision and  <math>w</math> is the amount decision, standard Tobit model assumes:

: <math>s=1[x\beta +u>0];</math>

: <math>w=x\beta+u.</math>

To make the model compatible with more contexts, a natural improvement is to assume:

: <math>s=1[x \gamma +u>0], \text{ where } u \sim N (0,1);</math>

<math>w=x\beta + e,</math> where the error term (<math>e</math>) is distributed as a [[truncated normal distribution]] with a density as <math>\varphi (\cdot) / \Phi \left(\frac{x\beta}\sigma \right)/\sigma;</math>

<math>s</math> and <math>w</math> are independent conditional on <math>x</math>.

This is called Truncated Normal Hurdle Model, which is proposed in Cragg (1971).<ref name="Cragg1971" /> By adding one more parameter and detach the amount decision with the participation decision, the model can fit more contexts. Under this model setup, the [[probability density function|density]] of the <math>y</math> given <math>x</math> can be written as:

: <math>f (y\mid x)= [1-\Phi (\chi\gamma)]^{1[y = 0]} \cdot \left[\frac{\Phi\ (\chi\gamma)}{\Phi ( \chi\beta/\sigma)} \left. \varphi \left(\frac{y-\chi\beta}{\sigma}\right) \right/ \sigma\right] ^{1[y>0]}</math>

From this density representation, it is obvious that it will degenerate to the standard Tobit model when <math>\gamma= \beta/\sigma.</math>  This also shows that Truncated Normal Hurdle Model is more general than the standard Tobit model.

The Truncated Normal Hurdle Model is usually estimated through MLE. The log-likelihood function can be written as:

: <math>
\begin{align}
\ell(\beta,\gamma,\sigma) = {} & \sum_{i=1}^N 1[y_i = 0] \log [1-\Phi (x_i \gamma) ] +1 [y_i>0] \log [\Phi (x_i \gamma)] \\[5pt]
& {} + 1[y_i>0] \left[ -\log \left[\Phi \left( \frac{x_i\beta} \sigma \right)\right] + \log \left(\varphi \left(\frac{y_i-x_i\beta} \sigma \right) \right) -\log (\sigma) \right]
\end{align}
</math>

From the log-likelihood function, <math>\gamma</math>  can be estimated by a [[probit model]] and <math>(\beta,\sigma)</math> can be estimated by a truncated normal regression model.<ref>Wooldridge, J. (2002): Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data, MIT Press, Cambridge, Mass, pp 692-694.</ref> Based on the estimates, consistent estimates for the Average Partial Effect can be estimated correspondingly.
